content: Israel's approach to animal welfare is governed by the Animal Welfare Law of 1994, which consists of two main components: the Animal Protection Law and the Animal Experimentation Law. This legislation was introduced by Abraham Poraz and was passed by the Knesset on January 11, 1994. Additional regulations under the Animal Protection Law include the establishment of the Animal Welfare Fund in 1995 and the introduction of permit requirements for organizing animal exhibitions and competitions in 2001. Furthermore, four other laws are relevant to animal welfare in Israel: the Wildlife Protection Law of 1955, the Animal Disease Ordinance of 1985, the Dog Regulation Law of 2002, and the Rabies Regulations (Vaccinations) of 2005. The Minister of Agriculture in Israel is tasked with enforcing the Animal Welfare Law, while the Minister of the Environment appoints trustees who are authorized to file complaints against individuals violating the law. The Animal Welfare Fund was created to support education, disseminate information, and provide assistance to animal welfare organizations. Between 2005 and 2006, approximately 3.5 million NIS (equivalent to $782,000 or €616,500) were allocated to animal welfare initiatives. These projects included educational programs, the appointment of animal welfare trustees, efforts to reduce the population of stray animals, promotion of animal adoption, support for the Israel Police in animal-related cases, responses to public requests for assistance with animals in distress, special projects, financial aid to animal welfare organizations, and participation in Knesset discussions. The Animal Experimentation Law regulates the use of animals in research and establishes a 23-member National Council for Animal Experimentation. This council has the authority to prohibit animal experiments if a reasonable alternative exists. However, animal rights organizations, such as CHAI (Concern for Helping Animals in Israel), argue that alternatives are rarely explored and that the law primarily serves the interests of academic researchers, pharmaceutical companies, and the government, rather than prioritizing animal welfare. The Wildlife Protection Law of 1955 was enacted to align with the standards of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES). This law prohibits the hunting of wild animals using traps, snares, nets, or poisons. The Animal Disease Ordinance of 1985 addresses issues related to animal health. The Dog Regulation Law of 2002 mandates that all dogs aged three months or older must be licensed, microchipped, and vaccinated against rabies. It also regulates the importation and ownership of dangerous dog breeds. The Rabies Regulations of 2005 further emphasize the importance of routine rabies vaccinations. In 1994, Israel implemented a new law enforcement policy aimed at reducing animal cruelty. Police stations were instructed to investigate reports of animal abuse, and an educational program was introduced in schools, proposing a weekly one-hour class discussion on the topic. Israel has also enacted several bans to protect animals. These include prohibitions on animal dissections in elementary and secondary schools (although optional participation in dissections is allowed at the university level), the use of trained animals in circus performances, and the production of foie gras. The ban on foie gras production is particularly notable, as Israel was previously the fourth-largest producer of foie gras globally but chose to forgo this significant source of income for ethical reasons. Additionally, the state prohibits killing animals with poison, forcing unfit animals to work, and overworking animals to the point of exhaustion. Although Israel has never engaged in whaling, it joined the International Whaling Commission to vote against the resumption of commercial whaling. In May 2001, eight individuals claiming to be animal rights activists sent a death threat via fax to Shraga Segal, an immunologist and former dean of Ben-Gurion University's medical school. The threat targeted Segal and his family after he appeared on a television talk show discussing animal experimentation alongside Likud party member Dani Naveh. Segal, who was a member of the National Council for Animal Experimentation, opposed Naveh's proposal to increase the representation of animal rights and welfare activists on the council. At the time, activists accounted for only three of the council's 23 members. Naveh had advocated for increasing their representation to half of the council.
